title: Depart from me (Luke 5:1–11)
hook: after the great catch Peter falls down: I am a sinful man

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth, read from Isaiah, and claimed the title Christos, the anointed one. Your line was good news to the poor. Who came to mind when you heard it? Day four hundred fifty-two.

Fishermen on the lake of Genesareth worked at night, when the fish came up toward the surface. So picture the morning. Simon and his partners have been out all night and caught nothing. They're on the shore, washing their nets, tired and done. A crowd presses in on a teacher, and the teacher climbs into Simon's boat and asks him to push off a little, so he can talk to the people from the water. Then, when he's finished, he says something no tired fisherman wants to hear: go back out. Put down your nets again. In the daytime. Today, what happens when Simon says yes.
screen: `ALL NIGHT, NOTHING.` → `A TEACHER IN SIMON'S BOAT.` → `PUT OUT INTO THE DEEP.`

segments.voice: Simon's answer is honest and a little weary: "Master, we have laboured all the night, and have taken nothing: but at thy word I will let down the net." He goes anyway. And the nets fill so full they begin to break. He waves for the other boat, James and John, and both boats load up until they start to sink. Now, you'd expect a fisherman to celebrate. This is the best morning of his working life. Instead Luke says Simon Peter fell down at Jesus' knees, saying: "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord." That's today's word, and it's strange. Nobody accused Peter of anything. The catch didn't scold him. But being that close to something holy made him see himself clearly, and what he saw made him want distance. People have felt this in many places in the Bible: Isaiah in the Temple cries out that he is a man of unclean lips. And Jesus doesn't argue with Peter about whether he's a sinner. He doesn't leave, either. He says: "Fear not: from henceforth thou shalt catch men." Peter asks for distance and gets a job. Then Luke adds a quiet line: they brought their boats to land, and leaving all things, they followed him. Catholics hear an echo of this moment at every Mass. Just before Communion, the people say they are not worthy to receive the Lord, and ask him only to say the word. Those words come from a Roman centurion a little later in Luke, but the instinct is Peter's on the beach: I'm not ready for you to come this close. And the answer, in both stories, is that he comes anyway.
screen: `AT THY WORD I WILL LET DOWN THE NET.` · `THE NETS BREAK, THE BOATS SINK.` · `PETER ASKS FOR DISTANCE.` · `FEAR NOT: YOU'LL CATCH PEOPLE.` · then, large: `DEPART FROM ME, FOR I AM A SINFUL MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let God come close anyway. Settle, and breathe. Notice one thing in you that makes you want to keep God, or anyone good, at arm's length. A habit, a regret, a mood you're in today. Don't fix it. Just name it, the way Peter named his. Then picture the answer he got: not a lecture, just fear not, and an invitation to stay in the boat. Breathe with that for a while. If you pray, you can say Peter's words, and then rest in the silence after them. The bell holds the time.
Genesareth. The lake where Peter's great catch left him saying depart from me, until Jesus answered, fear not. Today's word.
Your line: fear not. Today, when you catch yourself thinking you're too much of a mess for something good, say the line and stay put. Day four hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke's call of Peter at Sunday Mass in the year Luke's Gospel is read, and before Communion the whole congregation says aloud that they are not worthy, asking the Lord only to say the word.

fork.setup: you're Simon. you fished all night and caught nothing. a teacher tells you to go back out in daylight. what do you do?
options: explain politely that it's the wrong time of day.
say we caught nothing, but at your word I'll let down the net.
fork.reveal: he says both things at once: the honest complaint and the yes. the nets fill until they break.

original.note: Greek: fear not, or stop being afraid. Jesus' answer to Peter in Luke 5:10.

trapdoor: what you thought: Peter asked Jesus to leave because he was annoyed.
what it means: being near the holy showed Peter himself, and he felt unworthy. Jesus answers with fear not and a calling.
what a scholar hears: Luke's word for the catch of men, zogron, means taking alive: it's a net that rescues, not a hook that kills.

sources.ref: Order of Mass, invitation to Communion

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 5:5, 5:8 and 5:10 (punctuation and 'laboured').
The claim that fishermen on the lake worked at night is a common background note; confirm.
Trapdoor: the Greek of Luke 5:10 is zogron (zogreo, to take alive); confirm the gloss.
The Mass's 'Lord, I am not worthy' is paraphrased (current English Missal text is not public domain).
